item.question: Two triangles have BC = YZ = 5 cm, angle B = angle Y = 50 degrees and angle C = angle Z = 30 degrees. Are they congruent? Can there be triangles with these measurements that are not congruent? Construct one and find out.
steps: Draw BC = 5 cm. At B, measure 50 degrees from BC and draw a long ray.
At C, measure 30 degrees from CB on the same side and draw a long ray. The two rays head towards each other.
The rays cross at one point, and that point is A. Two straight lines that are not parallel cross only once, so A has only one possible place.
The angle at A is 180 - 50 - 30 = 100 degrees, the same for every child, and the triangles land exactly on one another.
So no triangle with these measurements can differ from another. The side BC sits between the two angles, which is why the rule is called A S A.
item.answer: Yes. The side and the two angles at its ends leave only one place for the third corner, so all such triangles are congruent.

item.question: Two triangles ABC and XYZ have angle A = angle X = 35 degrees, angle C = angle Z = 75 degrees and BC = YZ = 4 cm. The side is not between the two given angles. Are the triangles congruent? Find the missing angles B and Y.
steps: The three angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees, so a third angle is 180 minus the other two.
The two given angles add to 35 + 75 = 110 degrees.
Angle B = 180 - 110 = 70 degrees, and angle Y = 70 degrees in the same way.
Now BC lies between angle B and angle C, and YZ lies between angle Y and angle Z.
Angle B = angle Y, BC = YZ and angle C = angle Z, so the triangles are congruent by A S A: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle XYZ.
This case is called A A S, for angle, angle, side, and it guarantees congruence.
item.answer: Congruent. Angle B = angle Y = 70 degrees, then A S A gives triangle ABC congruent to triangle XYZ. The A A S condition guarantees congruence.

Angle $AOB$ and angle $DOC$ face each other where the two lines cross, so they are vertically opposite and equal.
Two sides and the angle between them match, so by $SAS$ triangle $AOB$ is congruent to triangle $DOC$.
$AB$ and $DC$ are corresponding sides of twin triangles, so $AB = CD$.

item.question: Two triangles each have a right angle, a base of 4 cm next to it and a long side of 5 cm opposite it. Are they congruent? Construct the triangle and find out whether different triangles can exist.
steps: Draw the base QR of 4 cm.
At Q, draw a long straight line at a right angle to QR.
Set the compass to 5 cm, put it at R and swing an arc. It cuts the upright line at a point above Q.
Mark that point P and join P to R. Triangle PQR has a right angle at Q, QR = 4 cm and PR = 5 cm.
Anyone who follows these steps gets this triangle, and the upright side PQ comes out as 3 cm.
item.answer: Yes. Every triangle built from a right angle, a 4 cm base and a 5 cm long side is the same triangle, so they are congruent.

3. Set the compass to 5 cm, put it at R and swing an arc. It cuts the upright line at a point above Q.

Answer: Yes. Every triangle built from a right angle, a 4 cm base and a 5 cm long side is the same triangle, so they are congruent.

item.question: Carry the upright line downwards below the base. Would the arc cut it there too? Is the triangle below also congruent to triangle PQR?
steps: Extend the upright line below QR. The same arc of 5 cm from R cuts it again, at a point P'.
That makes a second triangle P'QR, with the right angle at Q, QR = 4 cm and P'R = 5 cm.
Fold the paper along QR. P lands exactly on P', so triangle PQR lands on triangle P'QR.
The two landings are on opposite sides of the base, so the second triangle is the first one flipped, and a flip is allowed.

So there is only one triangle, and any two triangles with a right angle, a 4 cm side and a 5 cm long side are congruent. The long side opposite the right angle is the hypotenuse, and this condition is called RHS.
item.answer: Yes. The arc cuts the line below as well, and triangle P'QR is triangle PQR flipped over QR, so the two are congruent.

item.question: Triangle ABC is isosceles with AB equal to AC, and the angle at A is 80 degrees. What can we say about angle B and angle C? Draw the altitude from A to BC and use it.
steps: Draw the line from A straight down to BC, at a right angle to it, and call the foot D.
Pull the two triangles apart: triangle ADB and triangle ADC.
AB = AC is given, the angles at D are both 90 degrees by construction, and AD is a side of both triangles.
A right angle, the longest side and one more side match, so triangle ADB is congruent to triangle ADC by RHS.
Matching parts of twins are equal, so angle B = angle C.
item.answer: Angle B equals angle C. In a triangle, the angles opposite the equal sides are equal.

item.question: In an equilateral triangle ABC all three sides are equal. What can we say about its angles?
steps: AB = AC, so the triangle is isosceles with those two sides, and the angles opposite them are equal: angle B = angle C.
AB = BC as well, so the triangle is isosceles in a second way, and the angles opposite them are equal: angle A = angle C.
So angle A = angle B = angle C: all three angles are equal.
The three angles add up to 180 degrees, so 3 × angle = 180 and each angle is 180 / 3 = 60 degrees.
item.answer: All three angles are equal, and each one is 60 degrees.

item.question: What could the measures of the angles of an equilateral triangle be? Check your answer by drawing one.
steps: The reasoning says each angle is 60 degrees.
Draw a base BC of 5 cm. At B draw a ray at 60 degrees, and at C draw a ray at 60 degrees on the same side.
The rays meet at a point A. Measure AB and AC: both come out at 5 cm, so all three sides are equal.
Measure the angle at A: it is 60 degrees as well, so the drawing agrees with the reasoning.
item.answer: Each angle is 60 degrees, and a triangle drawn with two 60 degree angles on a base really has three equal sides.

item.question: Describe the congruent triangles you see in each of the five pictures.
steps: Louvre pyramid: the four sloping glass faces are congruent triangles, and each face is made of many small congruent triangular panes.
Pyramid of Giza: the four sloping faces are congruent triangles.
Dome: it is built from many congruent triangular panels, repeated all over its surface.
Rangoli: the star is made from one triangle repeated, and each copy is turned by the same amount about the centre, so the copies are congruent by turning.
Howrah Bridge: the truss is a line of congruent triangles, each identical to the next, and that is what gives the bridge its strength.
item.answer: Each structure repeats one triangle: four faces on each pyramid, many panels on the dome, turned copies in the rangoli, and a line of identical triangles in the bridge truss.
